questions.code: print([x * x for x in range(6) if x % 2 == 0], {x % 3 for x in range(7)})
questions.explanation: The list comprehension keeps the squares of the even numbers 0, 2, 4: [0, 4, 16]. The set comprehension collects x % 3 for x in 0..6: 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, which is the set {0, 1, 2}. Both build their result in O(n) time and space.

questions.code:
g = (x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3])
print(sum(g), sum(g))
questions.explanation: A generator expression is a one-shot iterator. The first `sum(g)` consumes it (2 + 4 + 6 = 12). The second `sum(g)` finds it already exhausted and returns 0. Generators use O(1) memory but cannot be rewound.

`zip` stops at the shortest input, so "abc" and [1, 2] give two pairs. `zip(*pairs)` unpacks the pairs as arguments and so transposes them: the first items together, then the second items. Each call is O(n).

`any` of an empty iterable is False and `all` of an empty iterable is True (vacuous truth). `any([0, "", None])` is False because every item is falsy. `all([1, "x", [0]])` is True because a non-empty list is truthy even if it contains a falsy item.

questions.prompt: square_count([1, 2, 3]) raises an error instead of returning 3. What is the bug?
options: Generator expressions must use square brackets
`nums` was already consumed by the loop
A generator expression has no len(); build a list, or count with sum(1 for _ in ...)
questions.explanation: Parentheses create a lazy generator, which has no length: `len(sq)` raises TypeError. Use a list comprehension (O(n) space) or `sum(1 for _ in sq)` (O(1) space, consumes the generator). Time is O(n) either way.

questions.prompt: first_even_index([3, 5, 4]) should return 2 (the 0-based position) but returns 3. What is the bug?
options: `enumerate(nums, 1)` starts counting at 1; drop the start argument
The loop must use `range(len(nums))`, because enumerate cannot be used with return
questions.explanation: The second argument of enumerate is the starting number of the counter, so every index is one too big. Use `enumerate(nums)` for 0-based positions. The scan is O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: What are the time and extra space of this function for a list of n numbers?
questions.code:
def sum_squares(nums):
    return sum([x * x for x in nums])
options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: The square brackets build the whole list of n squares before `sum` runs, so extra space is O(n). Writing `sum(x * x for x in nums)` (a generator expression) feeds the values to sum one at a time and needs O(1) extra space, with the same O(n) time.

questions.prompt: How does a list comprehension differ from a generator expression?
options: The generator expression is faster because it is compiled to C
The list comprehension is lazy and the generator expression builds a list
The list comprehension builds every result immediately and can be reused; the generator expression produces values lazily and can be consumed only once
They are identical except for the brackets used
questions.explanation: `[f(x) for x in it]` runs to completion and stores all n results (O(n) space). `(f(x) for x in it)` returns an iterator that computes one value per request (O(1) space) and is empty after one pass. Use a generator when you only loop once, for example inside `sum`, `any` or `all`.

questions.prompt: Transpose a matrix m (a list of rows) into a list of columns using idiomatic Python. Which expression does that?
questions.explanation: `zip(*m)` unpacks the rows as separate arguments, so zip pairs up their first items, then their second items, and so on: the columns, as tuples. Wrapping each in `list(...)` gives lists. `zip(m)` just wraps each row in a 1-tuple and `row[::-1]` reverses each row. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n).

questions.prompt: Check whether every word in a list is a palindrome, stopping at the first word that is not. Which expression does that?
options: all([w == w[::-1] for w in words])
any(w != w[::-1] for w in words)
sum(w == w[::-1] for w in words) == 0
all(w == w[::-1] for w in words)
questions.explanation: `all` over a generator expression short-circuits: it stops at the first False and never checks the rest. The list version `all([...])` builds the whole list first, so it checks every word. The other two expressions answer different questions (`any(w != ...)` is True when some word is NOT a palindrome). Worst case O(total length), best case O(length of the first bad word).
